name: Learn: Deployment Rollouts (modify existing)
objective: CKAD › Application Deployment (20%). Goal: operate Deployments that ALREADY exist — scale them, roll out a new image, roll back a bad release, change the update strategy, and inject config — the way the exam hands you a running app and asks you to change it.
description: Four Deployments are pre-seeded and running in the 'deploy-learn' namespace. You don't create them — you modify them: scale, rolling update, rollback, strategy, and config injection.

questions.title: Scale an existing Deployment
questions.teach:
Most real (and exam) work is changing a Deployment that's **already running**, not creating one. Scaling changes only the replica count — it does **not** change the pod template, so it does not trigger a rollout.

**Ways to scale:**
- `kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=N` — the fast path.
- `kubectl scale deployment/<name> --current-replicas=2 --replicas=5` — only scales if it's currently 2 (safe conditional).
- `kubectl edit deployment <name>` or `kubectl patch … -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'` — declarative edits.
- `kubectl apply -f` an updated manifest.

**Gotchas:**
- If a **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** targets the Deployment, it overrides manual `scale` within seconds — remove/adjust the HPA first.
- Scaling touches the `scale` subresource / `.spec.replicas`; it never rolls pods (no template change).
- `readyReplicas` lagging `replicas` just means pods are still starting — re-check, it's not a failure.
- Scaling to 0 is a valid way to 'pause' a workload without deleting it.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `deploy-learn`, the Deployment `frontend` already exists with 2 replicas. Scale it to **4**.

Target: `frontend` has 4 ready replicas.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn scale deployment/frontend --replicas=4`, then `kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy frontend`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn scale deployment/frontend --replicas=4
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy frontend   # 4/4 ready

verification.description: existing frontend scaled to 4 ready replicas

questions.title: Roll out a new image on an existing Deployment
questions.teach:
Changing the pod template (here, the container image) bumps the Deployment's generation and triggers a **rolling update** — a new ReplicaSet scales up while the old scales down, keeping the app available.

**Ways to change the image / trigger a rollout:**
- `kubectl set image deployment/<name> <container>=<newimg>` — targeted image swap. The **container name must match** — check it with `kubectl get deploy <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}'` (it is NOT always the deployment name).
- `kubectl edit deployment <name>`, `kubectl patch`, or re-`apply` an edited manifest.
- `kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>` — re-roll with no spec change (e.g. to pick up a changed ConfigMap/Secret).
- `kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>` to watch; `rollout pause`/`resume` to batch several edits into one rollout.

**Gotchas:**
- A rollout happens **only** if `.spec.template` actually changes — editing replicas or labels outside the template won't roll.
- Tune `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate` with `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable` (number or %).
- `--record` is deprecated — set a `kubernetes.io/change-cause` annotation to label the revision in history.
- The old ReplicaSet is kept (scaled to 0) for rollback — that history is your undo button.
questions.prompt:
The Deployment `api` in `deploy-learn` runs `nginx:1.25`. Perform a rolling update to `nginx:1.26` and wait for the rollout to finish.

Target: the update to `nginx:1.26` is rolled out (a new revision is recorded in `api`'s history) — this evidence persists even after you roll back in the next step.
questions.hint: Check the container name first (`kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].name}'`), then `kubectl -n deploy-learn set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.26` and `kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn set image deployment/api api=nginx:1.26
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout history deployment/api

verification.description: api rolling-updated to nginx:1.26 (recorded in history)

questions.title: Roll back a bad release
questions.teach:
Every rollout is recorded as a revision (one ReplicaSet per revision). `kubectl rollout undo` reverts the pod template to the previous revision — the standard fix when a new image misbehaves.

**Inspect and target revisions:**
- `kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>` lists revisions; `--revision=N` shows one revision's pod template.
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>` reverts to the previous revision (`--to-revision=0`).
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=N` targets a specific revision.
- The `kubernetes.io/change-cause` annotation is what fills the CHANGE-CAUSE column.

**Gotchas:**
- An undo is itself a **new rollout** — it creates a new revision; it does not delete the bad one from history.
- You can only roll back to revisions still kept by `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10); pruned ReplicaSets are gone.
- Rollback restores the **whole pod template** of that revision (image, env, resources…), not just the image.
- After an undo, re-check `kubectl rollout status` — the revert still rolls gradually per the strategy.
questions.prompt:
`nginx:1.26` is causing trouble. Roll back the `api` Deployment so its image returns to `nginx:1.25`.

Target: after the undo, `api`'s pod template image is `nginx:1.25` again and the rollout is complete (3/3).
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout undo deployment/api`, then `kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout undo deployment/api
kubectl -n deploy-learn rollout status deployment/api
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy api -o wide   # back to nginx:1.25

verification.description: api rolled back to nginx:1.25 (rollout complete)

questions.title: Change the update strategy
questions.teach:
`.spec.strategy` controls **how** a Deployment replaces pods on a template change.

**The two strategies:**
- `RollingUpdate` (default) — gradually replace pods, tuned by `maxSurge` (extra pods allowed above desired) and `maxUnavailable` (pods that may be down); both take a number or percent. Zero downtime, but two versions coexist briefly.
- `Recreate` — kill **all** old pods, then create the new ones. Brief downtime, but never two versions at once (needed when versions can't coexist, e.g. an incompatible schema).

**How to set it:**
- `kubectl edit deployment <name>` and set `.spec.strategy.type`.
- `kubectl patch deployment <name> -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'`.

**Gotchas:**
- `Recreate` must **not** carry a `rollingUpdate` block — set it to `null` or the API rejects it.
- `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` can't **both** be 0 (the rollout could never make progress).
- Changing the strategy alone does **not** trigger a rollout — it takes effect on the next template change.
questions.prompt:
The Deployment `cache` in `deploy-learn` uses the default RollingUpdate strategy. Change its update strategy to **Recreate**.

Target: `cache`'s `.spec.strategy.type` is `Recreate`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn patch deployment cache -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'` (or `kubectl edit` and set `strategy.type: Recreate`, removing the rollingUpdate block).
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn patch deployment cache -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate","rollingUpdate":null}}}'
kubectl -n deploy-learn get deploy cache -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}'   # Recreate

questions.title: Inject config into an existing Deployment
questions.teach:
You often modify a live Deployment's pod template to add env/config — which itself triggers a rolling update.

**`kubectl set` subcommands (fast, in-place template edits):**
- `kubectl set env deployment/<name> KEY=val` — add/overwrite an env var; `KEY-` removes one; `--list` prints current env; `--from=configmap/cm`/`--from=secret/s` injects all keys (envFrom).
- `kubectl set image deployment/<name> c=img` — change a container image.
- `kubectl set resources deployment/<name> --limits=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi --requests=…` — set requests/limits.
- `kubectl set serviceaccount deployment/<name> <sa>` — change the ServiceAccount.

**Gotchas:**
- `set env` on a Deployment edits the **template** → rolls the pods; `set env` targeting a bare Pod isn't allowed (pods are immutable there).
- `set env --from=configmap/<cm>` wires `envFrom` (all keys at once); a single key still needs `--keys` or an explicit `valueFrom`.
- Env from a ConfigMap/Secret is read **once at pod start** — changing the source later needs a `rollout restart` to take effect.
- `kubectl set env … --list` is the quick way to confirm what a container will receive.
questions.prompt:
Add an environment variable `TIER=backend` to the container in the `worker` Deployment (namespace `deploy-learn`).

Target: `worker`'s pod template has env `TIER` = `backend`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker TIER=backend`, then `kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --list` to confirm.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker TIER=backend
kubectl -n deploy-learn set env deployment/worker --list   # TIER=backend

verification.description: worker has env TIER=backend in its pod template
